articleHeadline: What You Need to Know About Zika Virus
articleSummary: Zika virus is transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes, and can spread via sexual contact, mother-to-fetus transmission, and blood transfusions. In pregnancy, Zika poses a risk of fetal microcephaly and other congenital abnormalities, miscarriage, or stillbirth. CDC guidance urges pregnant or breastfeeding individuals to avoid travel to areas with known transmission and recommends delaying conception after travel. articleHeadline: The plague never disappeared: these are the regions of the world where contracting Yersinia pestis is still possible.
articleSummary: Plague remains biologically incurable to eradicate, persisting as an enzootic disease in wild mammal reservoirs and their flea vectors, causing ongoing global reemergence. Yersinia pestis infects through a diverse reservoir of >200 mammal species (notably rodents) and >30 vector species, especially Xenopsylla cheopis, whose fleas amplify transmission. Three human forms are Bubonic (80–90%), septicemic, and Pneumonic—the latter being the most severe and, if untreated, near 100% fatal and directly transmissible via aerosols. Public health authorities classify plague as a mandatory reportable disease under IHR.

A September diphtheria vaccination campaign across five LGA—Kumbotso, Dala, Fagge, Gwale, Ungoggo—aims to curb transmission and protect vulnerable populations. Diphtheria spreads via respiratory droplets and close contact and can cause severe throat infections and breathing difficulties; vaccination, early detection, and prompt treatment are critical pending confirmation of the exact cause.
